rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبعري
rows.claim: The cited poem presents Mecca as an ancient inviolable sanctuary that no powerful visitor dares violate.
rows.anchor: كانت قديما لا يرام حريمها

rows.speaker: أبو قيس بن الأسلت الأنصاري المري
rows.claim: His poem recalls the elephant episode: the army was routed, an elephant was injured, and a showering wind scattered them like small bundles.
rows.anchor: فأرسل من فوقهم حاصبا … يلفهم

rows.speaker: أبو الصلت بن أبي ربيعة الثقفي
rows.claim: The poem says the elephant was immobilized at al-Mughammis, the force fled with broken legs, and the event remains among God's signs.
rows.anchor: حبس الفيل بالمغمس حتى … صار يحبو،

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: At Hudaybiyya the Prophet said the she-camel was held by the same power that had held the elephant, and promised to honor any proposal respecting God's sanctities; Bukhari alone transmits it.
rows.anchor: ما ذاك لها بخلق، ولكن حبسها

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: At the conquest of Mecca the Prophet said God had restrained the elephant from Mecca and granted the city to His Messenger and believers; its inviolability returned that day as before, with witnesses to inform absentees.
rows.anchor: إن الله حبس عن مكة الفيل، وسلط عليها رسوله والمؤمنين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir closes the commentary on the Elephant chapter after citing the conquest report.
rows.anchor: آخر تفسير سورة "الفيل".

rows.speaker: أم هانئ بنت أبي طالب
rows.claim: A rare report says God distinguished Quraysh in seven ways: the Prophet and prophethood, sanctuary offices, victory over the elephant, exclusive worship for ten years, and a Quraysh surah.
rows.anchor: وأن الله نصرهم على الفيل، وأنهم عبدوا الله، عز وجل،

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق وعبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: They connect the chapter to the preceding one: God stopped the elephant and destroyed its people so Quraysh could remain united and safe in their homeland.
rows.anchor: حبسنا عن مكة الفيل وأهلكنا أهله {لإيلاف قريش}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the familiarity as Quraysh's secure winter journey to Yemen and summer journey to Syria, protected by their status as residents of God's sanctuary.
rows.anchor: من الرحلة في الشتاء إلى اليمن، وفي الصيف إلى الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their safety at home is compared with the secure sanctuary surrounded by people who are seized; “for Quraysh's familiarity” explains the preceding favor.
rows.anchor: أولم يروا أنا جعلنا حرما آمنا ويتخطف الناس من حولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir treats the lām in “for Quraysh's familiarity” as appositional to the preceding clause and explanatory of it.
rows.anchor: {لإيلاف قريش} بدل من الأول ومفسر له.

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Al-Tabari instead reads the lām as one of exclamation: marvel at Quraysh's familiarity and God's favor, since Muslims agree these are separate surahs.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جرير: الصواب أن "اللام" لام التعجب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing of a protected sanctuary calls Quraysh to worship its Lord alone, as in the command to worship the Lord of the protected town.
rows.anchor: فليوحدوه بالعبادة، كما جعل لهم حرما آمنا وبيتا محرما،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God, Lord of the House, favored Quraysh with food after hunger, security after fear, and plentiful/cheap provision, so they must worship Him alone.
rows.anchor: تفضل عليهم بالأمن والرخص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obeying this command joins worldly and next-life security; disobedience removes both, as illustrated by a prosperous secure town punished with hunger and fear.
rows.anchor: جمع الله له بين أمن الدنيا وأمن الآخرة

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت يزيد
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet warns Quraysh in connection with their familiarity and urges them to worship the Lord who fed and secured them.
rows.anchor: ويل أمكم، قريش، لإيلاف قريش

rows.speaker: أم سلمة الأنصارية
rows.claim: A second report urges Quraysh to worship the Lord of the House who fed them and secured them; the text first gives its narrator as Usama b. Zayd.
rows.anchor: ويحكم يا معشر قريش، اعبدوا رب هذا البيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the second report's attribution to Usama is probably a copying or transmission error; it should be from Asma bint Yazid.
rows.anchor: وصوابه عن أسماء بنت يزيد بن السكن، أم سلمة الأنصارية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The religion” denied here means resurrection, recompense, and reward.
rows.anchor: وهو: المعاد والجزاء والثواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denier of recompense harshly oppresses the orphan, withholds the orphan's right, and neither feeds nor treats the orphan well.
rows.anchor: هو الذي يقهر اليتيم ويظلمه حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same person does not urge anyone to feed the needy poor who lack the means to sustain themselves.
rows.anchor: يعني: الفقير الذي لا شيء له يقوم بأوده وكفايته.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: They identify the threatened worshippers as hypocrites who pray publicly but do not pray in private.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وغيره: يعني المنافقين،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One explanation of being heedless of prayer is abandoning prayer altogether.
rows.anchor: كما قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: مسروق وأبو الضحى
rows.claim: Another explanation is letting the prayer's legally prescribed time expire.
rows.anchor: كما قاله مسروق، وأبو الضحى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase also covers habitually delaying prayer until the end of its time, neglecting its pillars or conditions, or lacking reverence and reflection; each incurs a share of the warning.
rows.anchor: فاللفظ يشمل هذا كله، ولكن من اتصف بشيء

rows.speaker: عطاء بن دينار
rows.claim: He notes the wording says heedless “of” their prayers, not heedless “within” prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء بن دينار: والحمد لله الذي قال:

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the canonical collections, the Prophet likens the hypocrite's prayer to waiting for sunset, then pecking out four units with little remembrance.
rows.anchor: يجلس يرقب الشمس، حتى إذا كانت بين قرني الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The example is the late Asr prayer, performed without calm or reverence and perhaps only for show, like the hypocrites described elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ولعله إنما حمله على القيام إليها مراءاة الناس،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report describes a valley in Hell that Hell itself seeks refuge from four hundred times daily, prepared for ostentatious people including a Qur'an-bearer, almsgiver, pilgrim, and fighter.
rows.anchor: أعد ذلك الوادي للمرائين من أمة محمد: لحامل كتاب الله.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Whoever publicizes his deed so people will hear of it will have God expose and disgrace him before creation.
rows.anchor: من سمع الناس بعمله، سمع الله به سامع خلقه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doing a deed for God and then feeling pleased when people see it does not count as ostentation, as a report promises reward for both secrecy and publicity.
rows.anchor: أن هذا لا يعد رياء

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a report Ibn Kathir calls strange through this chain, a man pleased that someone saw his prayer is told he has two rewards, for private and public worship.
rows.anchor: كتب لك أجران: أجر السر، وأجر العلانية

rows.speaker: ابن المبارك
rows.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak is quoted as calling the report a good hadith for people who ostentatiously perform deeds.
rows.anchor: نعم الحديث للمرائين

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says al-Kawthar is a river granted in Paradise, rich in goodness, where his community will gather on Judgment Day; its vessels number the stars and some people will be turned away for later innovations.
rows.anchor: هو نهر أعطانيه ربي، عز وجل، في الجنة، عليه خير كثير،

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A parallel Muslim report describes two channels from heaven feeding the Prophet's Basin from al-Kawthar, whose vessels number the stars.
rows.anchor: أنه يشخب فيه ميزابان من السماء عن نهر الكوثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many Qur'an readers infer that the chapter is Medinan from this report, and many jurists infer that its basmala is part of the chapter and was revealed with it.
rows.anchor: استدل به كثير من القراء على أن هذه السورة مدنية

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another Anas report describes al-Kawthar as a flowing river with pearl pavilions, musk-scented soil, and pearl-like stones.
rows.anchor: وإذا حافتاه قباب اللؤلؤ، فضربت بيدي في تربته، فإذا مسكه ذفرة

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Anas reports seeing in Paradise a river with pearl tents and fragrant musk; Gabriel identifies it as al-Kawthar granted by God.
rows.anchor: هذا الكوثر الذي أعطاكه الله، عز وجل

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In the night journey report transmitted by Bukhari and Muslim, Gabriel identifies a river with hollow pearl pavilions as al-Kawthar.
rows.anchor: أتيت على نهر حافتاه قباب اللؤلؤ المجوف

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says the river's ground is musk and its banks hold pearl and chrysolite palaces; Gabriel says the Lord reserved this river for the Prophet.
rows.anchor: هو الكوثر الذي خبأ لك ربك

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another report describes al-Kawthar's earth as musk, its water whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, and its birds with necks like camels.
rows.anchor: ترابه مسك، [ماؤه] (1) أبيض من اللبن،

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The river is described as whiter than milk and sweeter than honey, with birds whose necks resemble camels; their food is even more delightful.
rows.anchor: نهر في الجنة أعطانيه ربي، لهو أشد بياضا من اللبن،

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha says al-Kawthar is a great river given to the Prophet, with hollow pearls along its banks and vessels as numerous as stars.
rows.anchor: نهر [عظيم] (6) أعطيه نبيكم صلى الله عليه وسلم،

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report from Aisha says al-Kawthar lies in the center of Paradise, with pearl and ruby palaces, musk soil, and precious stones; Ibn Kathir notes the chain is interrupted.
rows.anchor: نهر في بطنان الجنة

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: A report says that anyone wishing to hear al-Kawthar's murmur should put fingers in their ears; Ibn Kathir says its link to Aisha is disconnected.
rows.anchor: من أحب أن يسمع خرير الكوثر، فليجعل أصبعيه في أذنيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas gives al-Kawthar the broad meaning of abundant good, which includes the Paradise river rather than excluding it.
rows.anchor: قال: الكوثر: الخير الكثير.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the abundant good of al-Kawthar extends through this world and the next.
rows.anchor: هو الخير الكثير في الدنيا والآخرة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima specifies al-Kawthar as prophethood, Qur'an, and the reward of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: هو النبوة والقرآن، وثواب الآخرة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers the broad interpretation because al-Kawthar comes from abundance; the river is one instance of the abundant good.
rows.anchor: لأن الكوثر من الكثرة، وهو الخير الكثير،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also explicitly identifies al-Kawthar as a Paradise river whose banks are gold and silver, whose bed is jewels, and whose water is whiter than snow and sweeter than honey.
rows.anchor: قال: الكوثر: نهر في الجنة، حافتاه ذهب وفضة،

rows.speaker: ابن عمر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports that al-Kawthar is a Paradise river with golden banks flowing over pearls and rubies.
rows.anchor: الكوثر نهر في الجنة، حافتاه من ذهب، يجري على الدر والياقوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir notes that al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Jarir also transmit the raised report.
rows.anchor: وهكذا رواه الترمذي، وابن ماجه، وابن أبي حاتم، وابن جرير،

rows.speaker: الترمذي
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi grades the raised report hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: به مرفوعا (3) وقال الترمذي: حسن صحيح.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In gratitude for abundant good, the Prophet is commanded to direct obligatory and voluntary prayer and sacrifice sincerely to God alone and sacrifice in His name.
rows.anchor: فأخلص لربك صلاتك المكتوبة والنافلة ونحرك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعطاء ومجاهد وعكرمة والحسن
rows.claim: They interpret “sacrifice” as slaughtering sacrificial camels and similar animals.
rows.anchor: يعني بذلك نحر البدن ونحوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sacrifices-for-God reading opposes pagan prostration to others and slaughter in another name.
rows.anchor: وهذا بخلاف ما كان المشركون عليه من السجود لغير الله

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: One reported interpretation puts the right hand over the left below the neck; Ibn Kathir says this attribution to Ali is unsound.
rows.anchor: يروى هذا عن علي، ولا يصح.

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الباقر
rows.claim: Al-Baqir is reported to interpret “sacrifice” as raising the hands when beginning prayer.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي جعفر الباقر: {وانحر} يعني: ارفع اليدين عند افتتاح الصلاة.

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Al-Tabari also records interpretations of putting the hands below the neck, raising them at the opening takbir, or facing the qibla with one's chest.
rows.anchor: وقيل: {وانحر} أي: استقبل بنحرك القبلة.

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A very weak report attributes to Ali a command to raise the hands at each takbir as the prayer's ornament; Ibn Kathir calls the report extremely objectionable.
rows.anchor: وإن لكل شيء زينة، وزينة الصلاة رفع اليدين عند كل تكبيرة.

rows.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
rows.claim: Ata al-Khurasani interprets “sacrifice” as straightening the back after bowing and raising the chest; Ibn Kathir judges this and the other alternatives very strange.
rows.anchor: أي: ارفع صلبك بعد الركوع واعتدل، وأبرز نحرك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers sacrifice of ritual offerings: the Prophet prayed Eid, then sacrificed, and said that sacrificing before prayer does not fulfill the rite.
rows.anchor: والصحيح القول الأول، أن المراد بالنحر ذبح المناسك؛

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says a man who sacrifices before the Eid prayer has only slaughtered meat; Abu Burda's case was exceptionally accepted and would not qualify anyone else.
rows.anchor: من صلى صلاتنا، ونسك نسكنا،

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Al-Tabari's preferred sense is to make all prayer and sacrifice purely for God, in gratitude for God's unmatched favor.
rows.anchor: فاجعل صلاتك كلها لربك خالصا دون ما سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir calls al-Tabari's synthesis excellent and notes that Muhammad b. Ka'b al-Qurazi and Ata had already stated it.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله في غاية الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's hater and hater of the guidance, truth, proof, and clear light he brought is the one cut off, low, and forgotten.
rows.anchor: هو الأبتر الأقل الأذل المنقطع ذكره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة
rows.claim: They say the verse was revealed about al-As b. Wa'il, who called the Prophet cut off because he had no surviving son.
rows.anchor: نزلت في العاص بن وائل

rows.speaker: محمد بن إسحاق عن يزيد بن رومان
rows.claim: Yazid b. Ruman explains that al-As b. Wa'il said Muhammad would be forgotten after death because he had no descendant.
rows.anchor: لا عقب له، فإذا هلك انقطع ذكره.

rows.speaker: شمر بن عطية
rows.claim: Shamr b. Atiyya says the verse was revealed about Uqba b. Abi Mu'ayt.
rows.anchor: نزلت في عقبة بن أبي معيط

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة
rows.claim: Another attribution names Ka'b b. al-Ashraf and a group of Quraysh disbelievers.
rows.anchor: نزلت في كعب بن الأشرف وجماعة من كفار قريش

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report with a sound chain says Quraysh told Ka'b b. al-Ashraf that Muhammad was severed from his people; Ka'b agreed they were superior, and the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: فنزلت: {إن شانئك هو الأبتر}

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says it was revealed about Abu Lahab, who told the polytheists that Muhammad was cut off after his son died.
rows.anchor: بتر محمد الليلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also says it was revealed about Abu Jahl and glosses “your hater” as your enemy.
rows.anchor: وعنه: {إن شانئك} يعني: عدوك.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima glosses “abtar” as a solitary or cut-off person.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: الأبتر: الفرد.

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Arabs called a man “cut off” when his sons died, which is what they said about Muhammad after his sons died.
rows.anchor: فلما مات أبناء رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قالوا: بتر محمد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the verse applies generally to everyone who hates the Prophet, and rejects the claim that his memory or religion would end: God made both endure.
rows.anchor: بل قد أبقى الله ذكره على رءوس الأشهاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chapter is Meccan, and Muslim reports that the Prophet recited it with al-Ikhlas in the two circumambulation prayers and in the two dawn sunnah units.
rows.anchor: قرأ بهذه السورة، وب " قل هو الله أحد " في ركعتي الطواف

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar says the Prophet repeatedly recited al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in the two units before dawn and after sunset; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
rows.anchor: قرأ في الركعتين قبل الفجر والركعتين بعد المغرب، بضعا وعشرين مرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet instructs Farwa b. Nawfal to recite al-Kafirun before sleeping, saying it is disavowal of shirk; Ahmad alone transmits this report.
rows.anchor: فإنها براءة من الشرك

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Reports attributed to the Prophet tell Jabala b. Haritha and al-Harith b. Jabala to recite the chapter to its end before sleep as disavowal of shirk.
rows.anchor: فإنها براءة من الشرك

rows.speaker: خباب
rows.claim: A report through al-Tabarani says the Prophet recited al-Kafirun through its end whenever he went to bed.
rows.anchor: كان إذا أخذ مضجعه قرأ: " قل يا أيها الكافرون " حتى يختمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chapter disavows the polytheists' practice and commands sincerity; its address embraces every disbeliever, though its immediate audience is Quraysh.
rows.anchor: شمل كل كافر على وجه الأرض، ولكن المواجهين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported occasion is Quraysh's ignorant proposal that the Prophet worship their idols for a year and they worship his God for a year.
rows.anchor: دعوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى عبادة أوثانهم سنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet rejects worship of Quraysh's idols and declares that they do not worship God alone; here “ma” means “the one who.”
rows.anchor: وهو الله وحده لا شريك له.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated wording also rejects following or imitating their invented worship; the Prophet worships as God loves and commands, whereas they follow desire rather than guidance.
rows.anchor: وإنما أعبد الله على الوجه الذي يحبه ويرضاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship requires both an object and a way of worship: the Messenger follows God's revealed way, while polytheists worship others without divine authorization.
rows.anchor: المشركون يعبدون غير الله عبادة لم يأذن بها الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final separation between religions parallels the command to maintain one's own deeds and leave theirs to them.
rows.anchor: لكم دينكم ولي دين

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: Al-Bukhari glosses “your religion” as unbelief and “my religion” as Islam.
rows.anchor: يقال: {لكم دينكم} الكفر، {ولي دين} الإسلام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation understands the lines as a refusal both now and for the rest of the Prophet's life, and says Quraysh will not worship what he worships.
rows.anchor: لا أعبد ما تعبدون الآن، ولا أجيبكم فيما بقي من عمري،

rows.speaker: ابن جرير عن بعض أهل العربية
rows.claim: One view treats the repeated clauses as emphasis, like the doubled assurance in al-Sharh and the repeated warning in al-Takathur.
rows.anchor: من باب التأكيد، كقوله: {فإن مع العسر يسرا

rows.speaker: البخاري وغيره من المفسرين
rows.claim: A second view assigns the first pair to the past and the second pair to the future.
rows.anchor: في الماضي، {ولا أنا عابد ما عبدتم ولا أنتم عابدون ما أعبد} في المستقبل.

rows.speaker: ابن تيمية
rows.claim: Ibn Taymiyya's fourth view distinguishes verbal denial of the act from the stronger nominal denial of accepting it, denying both occurrence and religious possibility.
rows.anchor: نفي قبوله لذلك بالكلية؛ لأن النفي بالجملة الاسمية آكد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir calls Ibn Taymiyya's interpretation a good one, alongside the initial interpretation.
rows.anchor: وهو قول حسن أيضا

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafi'i and others use this verse to treat all unbelief as one invalid religion for inheritance: Jews and Christians may inherit one another when kinship or another inheritance tie exists.
rows.anchor: الكفر كله ملة واحدة تورثه (2) اليهود من النصارى،

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Ahmad and his supporters deny reciprocal inheritance between Christians and Jews, citing the report that people of different religions do not inherit one another.
rows.anchor: لا يتوارث أهل ملتين شتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chapter is Medinan and, like al-Zalzalah, is said to equal a quarter of the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وهي مدنية. قد تقدم أنها تعدل ربع القرآن،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas confirms to Ubayd Allah b. Abd Allah that “When God's help and victory come” was the final complete surah revealed.
rows.anchor: تعلم آخر سورة من القرآن نزلت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the chapter as announcing the Prophet approaching death, and Umar says he knows no interpretation beyond this.
rows.anchor: هو أجل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أعلمه له،

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some Companions say the chapter commands praising God, thanking Him, and seeking forgiveness after victory.
rows.anchor: أمرنا أن نحمد الله ونستغفره إذا نصرنا وفتح علينا.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: An Ahmad report says that when the chapter came down, the Prophet knew his death had been announced.
rows.anchor: علم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قد نعيت إليه نفسه،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Tabarani reports that the chapter announced the Prophets death and that he then strove intensely for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: قال: فأخذ بأشد ما كان قط اجتهادا في أمر الآخرة.

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: When victory came, the Prophet welcomed people from Yemen as tenderhearted, gentle-natured people of faith, jurisprudence, and wisdom.
rows.anchor: قوم رقيقة قلوبهم، لينة قلوبهم، الإيمان يمان،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A further report says the chapter announced the Prophet's death and that he then exerted himself intensely in preparation for the afterlife.
rows.anchor: فأخذ بأشد ما كان قط اجتهادا في أمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: The report also links the arrival of victory and help with the coming of the people of Yemen.
rows.anchor: جاء الفتح ونصر الله، وجاء أهل اليمن

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that after the chapter came the Prophet said people were in one group and he and his Companions in another, and that after the conquest there is no emigration, only striving and intention.
rows.anchor: لا هجرة بعد الفتح، ولكن جهاد ونية

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saeed says Marwan called him a liar about the report, but Rafi b. Khadij and Zayd b. Thabit confirmed him despite fearing loss of their official posts.
rows.anchor: فقال أبو سعيد: لو شاء هذان لحدثاك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companions' reading that victory calls for praise, gratitude, prayer, and seeking forgiveness is sound and supported by the Prophet praying eight units at Mecca's conquest.
rows.anchor: أن نحمد الله ونشكره ونسبحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some jurists call the eight units at the conquest a special victory prayer and recommend that a commander pray it upon entering a conquered town; Sa'd did so at Ctesiphon.
rows.anchor: وإنما كانت صلاة الفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir says the better practice is to end the conquest prayer after each pair of units, based on a report in Abu Dawud.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه يسلم من كل ركعتين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعمر
rows.claim: They read the surah as announcing the Prophet's death: after Mecca's conquest and mass conversion, his worldly mission was complete, so he should prepare to meet God.
rows.anchor: فقد فرغ شغلنا بك في الدنيا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Nasa'i transmits that the Prophet took the surah as announcement of his death and thereafter applied himself intensely to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: نعيت لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم نفسه

rows.speaker: عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Aisha says the Prophet often said in bowing and prostration, “Glory and praise to You, our Lord; forgive me,” interpreting the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يكثر أن يقول في ركوعه وسجوده

rows.speaker: عائشة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Near the end of his life, the Prophet frequently glorified God, sought forgiveness, and repented; he said he had been ordered to do this when he saw the sign of this surah.
rows.anchor: وأمرني إذا رأيتها أن أسبح بحمده وأستغفره

rows.speaker: أم سلمة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Umm Salama says that near the end the Prophet repeated “Glory and praise be to God” in all his movements because he had been commanded to do so by this surah; Ibn Kathir calls the report strange.
rows.anchor: إني أمرت بها

rows.speaker: عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report says that whenever the Prophet recited the chapter and bowed, he repeatedly said, “Glory and praise to You, our Lord; forgive me; You are the Accepter of repentance.”
rows.anchor: سبحانك اللهم ربنا وبحمدك، اللهم اغفر لي إنك أنت التواب الرحيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The victory” here means the conquest of Mecca alone; Arab tribes delayed conversion until that decisive event, then entered Islam in crowds.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالفتح هاهنا فتح مكة قولا واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tribes reasoned that if Muhammad prevailed over his own people he must be a prophet; within two years the Arabian Peninsula had largely embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: إن ظهر على قومه فهو نبي

rows.speaker: عمرو بن سلمة
rows.claim: A Bukhari report says that after the conquest each tribe hastened to send its people to the Prophet to declare Islam.
rows.anchor: بادر كل قوم بإسلامهم إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن جابر
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say that people entered God's religion in crowds and will also leave it in crowds.
rows.anchor: إن الناس دخلوا في دين الله أفواجا، وسيخرجون منه أفواجا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet warned Quraysh from Mount Safa that a severe punishment was coming; Abu Lahab cursed him, and the chapter was revealed.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله: {تبت يدا أبي لهب وتب}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first clause is a prayer against Abu Lahab, while the second states as fact that he was ruined.
rows.anchor: الأول دعاء عليه، والثاني خبر عنه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Lahab was the Prophet's uncle, Abd al-Uzza b. Abd al-Muttalib, kunya Abu Utba; he was called Abu Lahab for his bright face and persistently abused the Prophet and his religion.
rows.anchor: وإنما سمي "أبا لهب" لإشراق وجهه،

rows.speaker: ربيعة بن عباد الديلي
rows.claim: Rabi'a recalls seeing the Prophet call people to profess God's oneness at the market of Dhu al-Majaz while his uncle followed, calling him a lying Sabian.
rows.anchor: هذا عمه أبو لهب

rows.speaker: ربيعة بن عباد الديلي عن أبيه
rows.claim: A parallel account says Abu Lahab followed the Prophet among tribes and warned them that he wanted them to abandon al-Lat and al-Uzza for a false innovation.
rows.anchor: هذا يريد منكم أن تسلخوا اللات والعزى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “May Abu Lahab's hands perish” means he failed and lost, his effort wasted; “and he perished” confirms his ruin.
rows.anchor: خسرت وخابت، وضل عمله وسعيه،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
rows.claim: They interpret Abu Lahab's “gain” as his children.
rows.anchor: {وما كسب} يعني: ولده.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that Abu Lahab hoped to ransom himself from Judgment Day punishment with his wealth and children, prompting the verse.
rows.anchor: فإني أفتدي نفسي يوم القيامة من العذاب بمالي وولدي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire has fierce sparks, flames, and intense burning.
rows.anchor: ذات شرر ولهيب وإحراق شديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His wife Umm Jamil, Arwa daughter of Harb and sister of Abu Sufyan, aided her husband's unbelief and hostility and will aid his punishment in Hell; she carried wood to cast onto him.
rows.anchor: فلهذا تكون يوم القيامة عونا عليه في عذابه

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعروة
rows.claim: Mujahid and Urwa interpret the cord around her neck as a cord of Hellfire.
rows.anchor: من مسد النار

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والحسن وقتادة والثوري والسدي
rows.claim: They say “carrier of firewood” means that she walked about spreading malicious gossip; al-Tabari prefers this explanation.
rows.anchor: كانت تمشي بالنميمة، [واختاره ابن جرير] (3) .

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وعطية الجدلي والضحاك وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say she placed thorns in the Prophet's path; al-Tabari also chose this view.
rows.anchor: كانت تضع الشوك في طريق رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers the gossip interpretation; the unsourced alternative says she mocked the Prophet's poverty while collecting firewood.
rows.anchor: والصحيح الأول، والله أعلم.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: She had a costly necklace and vowed to spend it in hostility toward Muhammad, so God replaced it with a cord around her neck.
rows.anchor: لأنفقنها في عداوة محمد

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi glosses “masad” as fiber.
rows.anchor: المسد: الليف.

rows.speaker: عروة بن الزبير
rows.claim: Urwa says the cord is a chain seventy cubits long.
rows.anchor: سلسلة ذرعها سبعون ذراعا

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawri calls it a necklace of fire seventy cubits long.
rows.anchor: هو قلادة من نار، طولها سبعون ذراعا.

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari defines masad as fiber or rope made of fiber, palm fronds, camel hide, or hair, and explains the verb as tightly twisting rope.
rows.anchor: المسد أيضا: حبل من ليف أو خوص،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the cord as an iron collar and notes that Arabs call the pulley “masad.”
rows.anchor: أي: طوق من حديد، ألا ترى أن العرب يسمون البكرة مسدا؟

rows.speaker: أسماء بنت أبي بكر
rows.claim: A report says Umm Jamil came raging with a stone to Abu Bakr while the Prophet sat unseen beside him, reciting a taunt; he was protected by a veil linked to 17:45.
rows.anchor: وإذا قرأت القرآن جعلنا بينك وبين الذين لا يؤمنون بالآخرة حجابا مستورا

rows.speaker: أم حكيم بنت عبد المطلب
rows.claim: When Umm Jamil stumbled while circling the House and cursed “Mudhammam,” Umm Hakim answered with a boast about her chastity, strength, and kinship.
rows.anchor: إني لحصان فما أكلم، وثقاف فما أعلم،
